summary: Following a review of the IETF meeting venue requirements, this document updates RFC 8718, clarifies how the IASA should interpret parts of it, and specifies a replacement exploratory meeting process, thereby updating RFC 8719.

eli5.summary: The group that holds big meetings reviewed its rules for choosing where to meet and tweaked them, including how to try out new places.

questions: how does the ietf choose meeting venues
what is an ietf exploratory meeting
what is an ietf overflow hotel
subtitle: The IETF tweaks its meeting venue rules: looser room blocks, a simpler exploratory meeting process and less ad hoc space.

tldr.problem: The venue rules in RFC 8718 and RFC 8719 were finished in 2018, and developments since then made some of them a poor fit for how meetings are actually booked and used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9712 replaces the exploratory meeting process, loosens the room block requirement, clarifies what 'close proximity' and 'Overflow Hotels' mean, and trims the ad hoc space requirements.
tldr.outcome: The IASA gets more flexibility in choosing cities and contracting rooms, and the rules better match what participants say they use. It updates RFC 8718 and RFC 8719 rather than replacing them.

facts.label: Old room block rule
facts.value: One-third or more of projected attendees

facts.label: New room block rule
facts.value: Sufficient rooms to meet the expected demand

today: RFC 9712 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 226) published in January 2025, and no later RFC has updated it. It updates RFC 8718 and RFC 8719.

sections.title: Why the Venue Rules Were Reviewed
sections.content:
IETF meeting venues are researched, negotiated, booked and managed under RFC 8718 (the venue selection process) and RFC 8719 (high-level guidance for the meeting policy). Both were published in 2020, but the substantive work was completed in 2018.

Since then, a number of developments have affected how well the model works. The IASA (IETF Administration Support Activity) reviewed venue selection, mainly informed by the staff who do the work, and found issues to fix through a mix of updates and clarifications of interpretation.
sections.eli5: The rules for choosing a meeting place were written a few years earlier. Things changed, so the organizers checked which rules still made sense.

sections.title: Summary of Changes
sections.content:
The document makes five changes to RFC 8718 and RFC 8719:

  • It updates the meeting (rotation) policy of RFC 8719 with a new process for choosing exploratory meetings.
  • It clarifies how to read 'close proximity' in RFC 8718.
  • It changes the room block requirement from 'one-third or more of projected meeting attendees' to 'sufficient rooms to meet the expected demand'.
  • It clarifies that Overflow Hotels are an entirely optional feature the IASA may provide at its own discretion.
  • It updates the ad hoc space requirements to match what post-meeting surveys say the community wants.
sections.eli5: There are five fixes. Some change a rule, and some just explain what a rule was always supposed to mean.

sections.title: Exploratory Meetings
sections.content:
RFC 8719 sets a '1-1-1-*' meeting policy: meetings rotate between North America, Europe and Asia, with the '*' allowing an occasional exploratory meeting. Under the old process a participant nominated a city, the community discussed it, and the IETF chair decided whether there was consensus that it was suitable.

RFC 9712 argues that community consensus is a very high bar. For ordinary meetings the IASA considers community feedback but makes the final call itself. Low attendance at some exploratory meetings also showed that consensus does not predict whether a city is viable.

The document therefore replaces Section 4 of RFC 8719. Exploratory meetings may be scheduled by the IASA through its normal processes, which include assessing the city, consulting the community, and deferring to the IESG if there is concern that the 'why we meet' objective of RFC 8718 might not be met. The IASA should keep exploratory meetings infrequent enough that they do not redefine 'exploratory' or disproportionately affect meetings in the 1-1-1 regions.
sections.eli5: Trying out a new city used to need everyone to agree first. Now the organizers decide it the same way they decide any other meeting, and they must not try new places too often.

sections.title: The One-Roof Preference and Close Proximity
sections.content:
RFC 8718 states a preference for 'One Roof', where qualified meeting space and guest rooms are in the same facility, and also requires the IETF Hotels to be in close proximity to the facility. Some in the community read 'One Roof' as the only way to meet the proximity requirement.

In practice the IASA books one of two configurations. A One-Roof venue can mean free meeting space with a large enough room block, a strong sense of community and a single point of contact, but few cities have such hotels and room rates are often high. A convention center with nearby hotels opens up many more cities and lower room rates, but it is harder to negotiate with, the IASA pays for the space, and the network arrangements are more complicated.

To avoid practically excluding many cities, the IASA should read 'close proximity' for a facility without an attached hotel as a walk of no more than ten minutes from the IETF Hotels to the meeting space, and the walk should be safe early in the morning and late at night.
sections.eli5: Having the hotel and the meeting rooms in one building is nice, but few cities have one. So a short, safe walk of ten minutes or less counts as close enough too.

sections.title: Room Blocks and Overflow Hotels
sections.content:
RFC 8718 required the IETF Hotels to have enough guest rooms for one-third or more of projected attendees. RFC 9712 explains that after COVID-driven disruption, hotels are more cautious, some require full payment in advance for room blocks, and large blocks no longer reliably get good discounts. Short-term apartment rentals also compete with hotels. The net result was that the IASA reserved more rooms than were used while guaranteeing occupancy levels, which created risk and wasted effort.

The requirement in Section 3.2.4 of RFC 8718 is therefore changed to 'sufficient rooms to meet the expected demand'.

Overflow Hotels are extra hotels with a negotiated group rate. They were historically contracted but were very underutilized, and are now rarely contracted. Because RFC 8718 mentions them, many still think they are a normal feature, so the IASA should treat any reference to them as an entirely optional feature that it may provide at its own discretion.
sections.eli5: The organizers used to book lots of hotel rooms that nobody slept in, and they had to pay for them. Now they only book as many as they expect people to need.

sections.title: Ad Hoc Space, the Lounge and the Terminal Room
sections.content:
RFC 8718 asked for enough places for ad hoc conversations in the facilities, hotels and bars or restaurants within a 5-10 minute walk, and for a lounge with a space for working online. A terminal room, Ethernet, a printer and a staffed help desk were long-standing features, though not a formal requirement.

Survey feedback showed that both the lounge and the terminal room are used regularly but far below capacity. Most participants want immediately accessible ad hoc space, which plenty of hallway seating provides, so the IASA now brings in extra hallway seating when the venue's is insufficient. There is still a need for quiet places to work between sessions.

Two bullets of RFC 8718 are rewritten. The ad hoc bullet in Section 3.2.2 now asks for 'sufficient, easily accessible places within the Facility for people to hold ad hoc conversations and group discussions'. The lounge bullet in Section 3.2.4 now asks for 'sufficient places within the Facility suitable for people to work online on their own devices'.
sections.eli5: People mostly chat in hallways, not in special lounges, so the rules now ask for good hallway seating and quiet spots to work.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content: The document has no IANA actions. Its Security Considerations section says only that it should not affect the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: These are meeting rules, not computer rules, so they do not change how safe the Internet is.
